claim: Mortality from triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) is significantly higher in African American (AA) women compared to White American (WA) women.
source: Mortality from triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) is significantly higher in African American (AA) women compared to White American (WA) women emphasizing ethnicity as a major risk factor
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by SEER database analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: AA-TNBC cells exhibit elevated growth compared to WA-TNBC cells.
source: AA-TNBC cells exhibited higher growth ranging from 2.5- to 4-fold (MDA-MB-468 – 2.5-fold, HCC1569 – 3-fold and HCC1806 – 4-fold) within 96 hr compared to WA-TNBC cells which exhibited growth ranging from 1.8- to 2.5-fold (Hs578t – 1.8-fold, HCC1937 – 2-fold, and BT549 – 2.5-fold) (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from cell viability assays shown in Figure 1G.

claim: AA-TNBC cells have higher migratory potential compared to WA-TNBC cells.
source: These results reveal that AA-TNBC cells have higher migratory potential compared to WA-TNBC cells.
evidence: Supported by scratch-migration and spheroid-migration assay data presented in Figure 1H-L.

claim: AA women have twice as high TNBC incidence (38/100,000) in comparison to WA women (19/100,000).
source: AA women have twice as high (38/100,000) TNBC incidence in comparison to WA women (19/100,000).
evidence: This is a factual statement about incidence rates presented in the introduction.

claim: The 5-year relative survival rate for TNBC is significantly lower in AA women (14%) compared to WA women (36%).
source: Not only do AA women have higher TNBC incidence, but the survival rate for TNBC is also significantly lower in AA women in comparison to WA women (5-year relative survival of only 14% for AA in comparison to 36% for WA).
evidence: This is a factual statement about survival rates presented in the introduction.

claim: AA-TNBC cells show elevated expression of embryonic stem cell markers NANOG, OCT4, SOX2, KLF4, and c-MYC compared to WA-TNBC cells.
source: In addition, AA-TNBC cells showed elevated expression of embryonic stem cell markers, NANOG, OCT4, SOX2, KLF4, and c-MYC, compared to WA-TNBC cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: AA-TNBC cells form higher number of mammospheres (~2-fold increase) compared to WA-TNBC cells.
source: Higher number of mammospheres (~2-fold increase) were formed by AA-TNBC cells in contrast to WA-TNBC cells which formed fewer mammospheres.
evidence: Supported by mammosphere formation assay data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: GLI1 and Notch1 pathways are enriched in AA-TNBC cells compared to WA-TNBC cells.
source: Meta-analysis of RNA-sequencing data of multiple AA- and WA-TNBC cell lines shows enrichment of GLI1 and Notch1 pathways in AA-TNBC cells.
evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing data analysis from CCLE database presented in Figure 3A and Figure 4A.

claim: There is a positive correlation between GLI1 and Notch1 in AA-TNBC tumors.
source: In line with this observation, analysis of TCGA dataset reveals a positive correlation between GLI1 and Notch1 in AA-TNBC and a negative correlation in WA-TNBC.
evidence: Supported by ssGSEA analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There is a negative correlation between GLI1 and Notch1 in WA-TNBC tumors.
source: In line with this observation, analysis of TCGA dataset reveals a positive correlation between GLI1 and Notch1 in AA-TNBC and a negative correlation in WA-TNBC.
evidence: Supported by ssGSEA analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Increased nuclear localization of GLI1 is observed in AA-TNBC cells compared to WA-TNBC cells.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis showed elevated nuclear accumulation of GLI1 in AA-TNBC cells compared to WA-TNBC cells (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Increased nuclear localization of Notch1 is observed in AA-TNBC cells compared to WA-TNBC cells.
source: Confocal microscopy detected higher nuclear accumulation of Notch1 in AA-TNBC compared to WA-TNBC cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: GLI1 and NICD exhibit physical interaction in AA-TNBC cells.
source: Immunoprecipitates with GLI1 antibody showed the presence of NICD while IgG controls were negative (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Combined inhibition of GLI1 and Notch1 synergistically inhibits AA-TNBC cells.
source: Analysis of the viability data using Compusyn software (Compusyn Inc,.Pramus, NJ) uncovered the synergistic effects of combination regimens (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,D,F).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data and combination index analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inhibition of GLI1 and Notch1 improves the efficacy of chemotherapy in AA-TNBC cells.
source: Of importance, inhibition of GLI1 and Notch1 synergistically improves the efficacy of chemotherapy in AA-TNBC cells.
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data showing synergistic effects of DAPT+GANT61 with doxorubicin/carboplatin in Figure 5H-K.

claim: Treatment with DAPT+GANT61+doxorubicin/carboplatin results in significant tumor regression in AA-TNBC-derived tumors.
source: Combined treatment of AA-TNBC-derived tumors with GANT61, DAPT, and doxorubicin/carboplatin results in significant tumor regression
evidence: Supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Triple-therapy-treated AA-TNBC tumors show reduced migration of tumor-dissociated cells.
source: Interestingly, tumor cells from triple-therapy treated groups exhibited significantly reduced transwell migration (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 5)
evidence: Supported by transwell migration assay data from tumor-dissociated cells shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Triple-therapy-treated AA-TNBC tumors show reduced invasion of tumor-dissociated cells.
source: Interestingly, tumor cells from triple-therapy treated groups exhibited significantly reduced transwell migration (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 5) and Matrigel invasion (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 6) compared to vehicle and single agent-treated groups.
evidence: Supported by Matrigel invasion assay data from tumor-dissociated cells shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Triple-therapy-treated AA-TNBC tumors show decreased mammosphere formation potential.
source: Decreased mammosphere formation was observed at all dilutions (500–8000 cells/well) for tumor cells from triple-therapy-treated group compared to vehicle and single agent-treated groups (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by mammosphere formation assay data from tumor-dissociated cells shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: Triple-therapy-treated AA-TNBC tumors show reduced CD44+/CD24- population.
source: Tumor-dissociated cells, examined for the presence of stemness marker CD44+/CD24-, showed higher stemness in vehicle-treated group (87.6%) compared to triple-therapy-treated tumors (48.6% for DGD and 65.2% in CGD) (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Secondary tumors derived from triple-therapy-treated AA-TNBC tumors show diminished stem-like phenotype.
source: Indeed, secondary tumors derived from triple-therapy-treated AA-TNBC tumors show diminished stem-like phenotype.
evidence: Supported by limiting dilution assay data showing reduced stem cell frequency in Figure 7D.

claim: TNBC tumors from AA women express significantly higher level of GLI1 compared to TNBC tumors from WA women.
source: Finally, we show that TNBC tumors from AA women express significantly higher level of GLI1 and Notch1 expression in comparison to TNBC tumors from WA women.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical analysis of clinical TNBC tissue samples shown in Figure 7G-I.

claim: TNBC tumors from AA women express significantly higher level of Notch1 compared to TNBC tumors from WA women.
source: Finally, we show that TNBC tumors from AA women express significantly higher level of GLI1 and Notch1 expression in comparison to TNBC tumors from WA women.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical analysis of clinical TNBC tissue samples shown in Figure 7G-I.

claim: AA women younger than 50 have 1.9–2.6 times higher breast cancer-related mortality compared to WA women.
source: AA women younger than 50 have 1.9–2.6 times higher breast cancer-related mortality compared to WA women, which declines to 1.1–1.2 times higher in 70–89 age-group (DeSantis et al., 2019; Siegel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a factual statement supported by citations to published literature.

claim: AA tumors show higher prevalence of TP53 mutations (42.9% vs. 27.6%) compared to WA tumors.
source: Comparative assessment of the genomic landscape of breast tumors from AA and WA women reveals that AA tumors show higher prevalence of TP53 mutations (42.9% vs. 27.6%) and lower level of PIK3CA mutations (20.0% vs. 33.9%) in comparison WA tumors.
evidence: This is a factual statement about genomic differences presented in the introduction.

claim: AA tumors show lower level of PIK3CA mutations (20.0% vs. 33.9%) compared to WA tumors.
source: Comparative assessment of the genomic landscape of breast tumors from AA and WA women reveals that AA tumors show higher prevalence of TP53 mutations (42.9% vs. 27.6%) and lower level of PIK3CA mutations (20.0% vs. 33.9%) in comparison WA tumors.
evidence: This is a factual statement about genomic differences presented in the introduction.

claim: Elevated expression of GLI1 and GLI1-responsive genes strongly associates with poor recurrence-free survival in TNBC patients.
source: Kaplan–Meier analysis showed that elevated expression of GLI1 and GLI1-responsive genes strongly associated with poor recurrence-free survival in TNBC patients (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: High Notch1 expression strongly associates with poor recurrence-free survival in TNBC patients with hazard ratio of 1.97.
source: Strong association between high Notch1 expression and poor RFS was observed with hazard ratio of 1.97 (p = 0.0021) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: GLI1 overexpression increases NICD transactivation in AA-TNBC cells.
source: Cells overexpressing GLI1 exhibited increased NICD transactivation in a luciferase assay (Figure 5D)
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: GLI1 overexpression increases expression of Notch-responsive genes Hes1 and Hey1.
source: Cells overexpressing GLI1 exhibited increased NICD transactivation in a luciferase assay (Figure 5D) and also showed increased expression of Notch-responsive genes – Hes1 and Hey1 (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Notch1 overexpression increases expression of GLI1-responsive gene FOXM1.
source: Notch1 overexpression also led to increased expression of GLI1-responsive gene – FOXM1 (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: AA-TNBC (HCC1806) tumors show more effective growth inhibition in response to DAPT + GANT61 compared to chemotherapy combination.
source: AA-TNBC (HCC1806) tumors showed more effective growth inhibition in response to DAPT + GANT61 in comparison to chemotherapy combination whereas WA-TNBC (HCC1937 and MDA-MB-231) tumors showed enhanced growth inhibition in response to doxorubicin + carboplatin combination.
evidence: Supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: WA-TNBC tumors show enhanced growth inhibition in response to doxorubicin + carboplatin combination compared to DAPT + GANT61.
source: AA-TNBC (HCC1806) tumors showed more effective growth inhibition in response to DAPT + GANT61 in comparison to chemotherapy combination whereas WA-TNBC (HCC1937 and MDA-MB-231) tumors showed enhanced growth inhibition in response to doxorubicin + carboplatin combination.
evidence: Supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: GANT61 + DAPT combination treatment does not reduce the growth of WA-TNBC cells-derived tumors.
source: GANT61 + DAPT combination treatment did not reduce the growth of WA-TNBC cells-derived tumors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The frequency of breast tumor-initiating cells in the CARBO + GANT61 + DAPT-treated tumor group was 1 in 1,178,112 cells compared to 1 in 70,160 cells in the control group at week 3.
source: The frequency of breast tumor-initiating cells in the CARBO + GANT61 + DAPT-treated tumor group (CGD) was determined to be 1 in 1,178,112 cells compared to 1 in 70,160 cells in the control group and CARBO-treated group at week 3.
evidence: Supported by limiting dilution assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Black women showed higher prevalence of grade 3 TNBC at the time of diagnosis compared to white women (83.1% vs. 77.98%) in SEER dataset.
source: Black women showed higher prevalence of grade 3 TNBC at the time of diagnosis compared to white women (83.1% vs. 77.98%) in SEER dataset (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by SEER database analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: AA-TNBC shows higher percentage (18.75%) of stage III tumors compared to WA-TNBC (11.76%) in TCGA data.
source: Analysis of the TCGA data indicated higher percentage of AA-TNBC (18.75%) with stage III tumors than WA-TNBC (11.76%) (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: HCC1806 and HCC1569 cells migrated at a speed of 3.1 and 2.8 µm/hr whereas Hs578t and HCC1937 migrated at a speed of 1.8 µm/hr in scratch-migration assay.
source: HCC1806 and HCC1569 migrated at a speed of 3.1 and 2.8 µm/hr whereas Hs578t and HCC1937 migrated at a speed of 1.8 µm/hr (Figure 1K).
evidence: Supported by scratch-migration assay data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: In spheroid-migration assay, HCC1806 and HCC1569 cells migrated an average distance of 29 and 27.72 µm while Hs578t and HCC1937 spheroids migrated 15.45 and 10.08 µm.
source: HCC1806 and HCC1569 cells migrated an average distance of 29 and 27.72 µm. In the case of Hs578t and HCC1937 spheroids, the distance traversed was 15.45 and 10.08 µm.
evidence: Supported by spheroid-migration assay data shown in Figure 1I and L.

claim: AA-TNBC cells exhibited higher migration rate (1.209 and 1.155 µm/hr for HCC1806 and HCC1569 cells) than WA-TNBC cells which migrated at a speed of 0.644 (Hs578t) and 0.42 µm/hr (HCC1937) in spheroid-migration assay.
source: AA-TNBC cells exhibited higher migration rate (1.209 and 1.155 µm/hr for HCC1806 and HCC1569 cells) than WA-TNBC cells which migrated at a speed of 0.644 (Hs578t) and 0.42 µm/hr (HCC1937) (Figure 1L).
evidence: Supported by spheroid-migration assay data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: GSEA of differentially expressed genes in AA-TNBC and WA-TNBC showed positive enrichment of epithelial mesenchymal transition pathway in AA-TNBC tumors.
source: Interestingly, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in AA-TNBC and WA-TNBC diagnosed between 1987 and 2007 (GSE46581 dataset) (Lindner et al., 2013) showed a positive enrichment of epithelial mesenchymal transition pathway and metastasis pathway in AA-TNBC tumors compared to WA-TNBC tumors (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis of GSE46581 dataset shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GSEA of differentially expressed genes in AA-TNBC and WA-TNBC showed positive enrichment of metastasis pathway in AA-TNBC tumors.
source: Interestingly, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in AA-TNBC and WA-TNBC diagnosed between 1987 and 2007 (GSE46581 dataset) (Lindner et al., 2013) showed a positive enrichment of epithelial mesenchymal transition pathway and metastasis pathway in AA-TNBC tumors compared to WA-TNBC tumors (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis of GSE46581 dataset shown in Figure 2A.

claim: RNA-sequencing data analysis revealed upregulation of embryonic stem cell pluripotency pathway in AA-TNBC cells compared to WA-TNBC cells.
source: Furthermore, analyses of the RNA-sequencing data of TNBC cell lines from Broad Institute Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE) (available with Expression Atlas of EMBL-EBI database) revealed an upregulation of an embryonic stem cell pluripotency pathway in MDA-MB-468, HCC1806, and HCC1569 (AA-TNBC) cells in comparison to HCC1937, BT20, MDA-MB-231, Hs578t, and BT549 (WA-TNBC) cells.
evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing data analysis from CCLE database.

claim: Increased expression of a set of 23 embryonic stemness-associated genes was noted in AA-TNBC cells compared to WA-TNBC cell lines.
source: Increased expression of a set of 23 embryonic stemness-associated genes was noted in AA-TNBC cells compared to WA-TNBC cell lines (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: AA-TNBC HCC1569 showed 80.7% CD44high/CD49fhigh breast cancer stem cells.
source: Higher population of CD44high/CD49fhigh breast cancer stem cell (BCSCs) was observed in AA-TNBC HCC1569 (80.7%) and HCC1806 (93.4%) while MDA-MB-468 cells showed slightly decreased levels (15.7%).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: AA-TNBC HCC1806 showed 93.4% CD44high/CD49fhigh breast cancer stem cells.
source: Higher population of CD44high/CD49fhigh breast cancer stem cell (BCSCs) was observed in AA-TNBC HCC1569 (80.7%) and HCC1806 (93.4%) while MDA-MB-468 cells showed slightly decreased levels (15.7%).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: WA-TNBC Hs578t exhibited 1.6% CD44high/CD49fhigh breast cancer stem cells.
source: Among WA-TNBC cells, Hs578t exhibited much lower levels of CD44high/CD49fhigh BCSCs (1.6%) whereas BT549 and HCC1937 cells showed slightly higher BCSCs (52.5% and 55.4%).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Higher expression of CD44, KLF4, MYC, and NANOG was observed in TNBC tumors from AA women compared to TNBC tumors from WA women in Affymetrix and TCGA datasets.
source: Furthermore, analysis of Affymetrix and TCGA datasets revealed higher expression of CD44, KLF4, MYC, and NANOG in TNBC tumors from AA women compared to TNBC tumors from WA women (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by analysis of Affymetrix and TCGA datasets shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Higher expression of GLI1-responsive genes CCNF, FOXM1, GSK3, and CDC34 was observed in TNBC tumors from AA women compared to WA women in Affymetrix and TCGA datasets.
source: In addition, higher expression of GLI1-responsive genes, CCNF, FOXM1, GSK3, and CDC34, was observed in TNBC tumors from AA women compared to WA women in Affymetrix and TCGA datasets (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by analysis of Affymetrix and TCGA datasets shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Higher expression of Notch1-responsive genes HEY1, HEY2, HES1, HES4, HES5, and HES6 was observed in AA-TNBC compared to WA-TNBC tumors in Affymetrix and TCGA datasets.
source: Further exploration of Notch1 signaling in Affymetrix and TCGA datasets showed higher expression of Notch1-responsive genes, HEY1, HEY2, HES1, HES4, HES5, and HES6, in AA-TNBC compared to WA-TNBC tumors (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by analysis of Affymetrix and TCGA datasets shown in Figure 4E.

claim: More than 4-fold higher nuclear accumulation of Notch1 was observed in AA-TNBC cells compared to WA-TNBC cells.
source: We observed more than 4-fold higher nuclear accumulation of Notch1 in AA-TNBC cells compared to WA-TNBC cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Treatment with 20 µM GANT61 led to 50% growth inhibition in AA-TNBC cells.
source: Treatment with 20 µM GANT61 led to 50% growth inhibition but no IC50 was achieved in the DAPT-treated AA-TNBC cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,C,E).
evidence: Supported by MTT cell viability assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: No IC50 was achieved in DAPT-treated AA-TNBC cells as single agent.
source: Treatment with 20 µM GANT61 led to 50% growth inhibition but no IC50 was achieved in the DAPT-treated AA-TNBC cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,C,E).
evidence: Supported by MTT cell viability assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: HCC1806 cells treated with 50 µM DAPT, 10 µM GANT61 in combination with varied concentration of doxorubicin exhibited a 10-fold reduced IC50 compared to doxorubicin monotherapy.
source: HCC1806 cells treated with 50 µM DAPT, 10 µM GANT61 in combination with a varied concentration of doxorubicin exhibited a 10-fold reduced IC50 in DOX + GANT61+ DAPT combination compared to doxorubicin monotherapy (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Treatment with 0.25 µM of carboplatin in combination with 50 µM DAPT and 10 µM GANT61 caused 50% cell death in HCC1806 cells while 40 µM carboplatin monotherapy did not achieve IC50.
source: While cells treated with 40 µM of carboplatin monotherapy did not achieve IC50, surprisingly, treatment with 0.25 µM of carboplatin in combination with 50 µM DAPT and 10 µM GANT61 caused 50% cell death in HCC1806 cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Tumor-dissociated cells from CARBO + GANT61 + DAPT-treated group exhibited reduced aldehyde dehydrogenase activity (17.7%) compared to vehicle (45.5%) and CARBO (40.3%).
source: Tumor-dissociated cells from CARBO + GANT61 + DAPT-treated group exhibited reduced aldehyde dehydrogenase activity (17.7%) in comparison to vehicle (45.5%) and CARBO (40.3%) (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by ALDEFLOUR assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Reduced percentage of ALDH+ cells were observed in CARBO + GANT61 + DAPT-treated group (2.5%) compared to vehicle (14.4%) and CARBO (10.4%).
source: Also, reduced percentage of ALDH+ cells were observed in CARBO + GANT61 + DAPT-treated group (2.5%) compared to vehicle (14.4%) and CARBO (10.4%) (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: CARBO + GANT61 + DAPT treatment resulted in reduced percentage of CD44+/CD24- and CD44+/CD49f+ cells in AA-TNBC tumors compared to vehicle and CARBO-treated group.
source: CARBO + GANT61 + DAPT treatment also resulted in reduced percentage of CD44+/CD24- and CD44+/CD49f+ cells in AA-TNBC tumors compared to vehicle and CARBO-treated group (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The disparity in TNBC-related survival in AA women vs. WA women is evident even after adjusting for socioeconomic status and access to medical care.
source: It is important to note that this disparity in TNBC-related survival in AA women vs. WA women is evident even after adjusting for socioeconomic status and access to medical care, strongly indicating a biological basis (Carey et al., 2006; Dietze et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: AA tumors show higher prevalence of TP53 mutations and lower level of PIK3CA mutations compared to WA tumors.
source: Comparative assessment of the genomic landscape of breast tumors from AA and WA women reveals that AA tumors show higher prevalence of TP53 mutations (42.9% vs. 27.6%) and lower level of PIK3CA mutations (20.0% vs. 33.9%) in comparison WA tumors.
evidence: This statement is based on comparative genomic assessment cited in the introduction.

claim: Greater intratumoral genetic heterogeneity including an enrichment of immortalization signature gene set is observed in AA tumors.
source: Greater intratumoral genetic heterogeneity including an enrichment of immortalization signature gene set is also observed in AA tumors (Andey et al., 2020; Keenan et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Distinct differences in multiple genes including CRYBB2, PSPHL, and SOS1 have been observed in AA vs. WA invasive breast cancer even after matching tumors for pathological characteristics.
source: Even after matching tumors for pathological characteristics, distinct differences in multiple genes including CRYBB2, PSPHL, and SOS1 have been observed in AA vs. WA invasive breast cancer (Field et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Several unique gene expression variations in breast tumors as well as tumor stroma are noted in AA that may support higher microvessel density and macrophage infiltration.
source: Several unique gene expression variations in breast tumors as well as tumor stroma are noted in AA that may support higher microvessel density and macrophage infiltration (Martin et al., 2009; Stewart et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature and involves speculation about biological implications.

claim: Several cell cycle regulators such as CDKN2A (p16), CCNA2, CCNB1, and CCNE2 express at a higher level in AA breast tumors.
source: While several cell cycle regulators such as CDKN2A (p16), CCNA2, CCNB1, and CCNE2 express at a higher level in AA breast tumors, a unique gene set comprising of PSPHL, CXCL10, CXCL11, ISG20, and GMDS is overexpressed in AA tumor stroma (Grunda et al., 2012; Martin et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A unique gene set comprising of PSPHL, CXCL10, CXCL11, ISG20, and GMDS is overexpressed in AA tumor stroma.
source: While several cell cycle regulators such as CDKN2A (p16), CCNA2, CCNB1, and CCNE2 express at a higher level in AA breast tumors, a unique gene set comprising of PSPHL, CXCL10, CXCL11, ISG20, and GMDS is overexpressed in AA tumor stroma (Grunda et al., 2012; Martin et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: No significant differences are reported in somatic mutations between AA-TNBC and WA-TNBC in a customized set of 151 genes.
source: No significant differences are reported in somatic mutations between AA-TNBC and WA-TNBC in a customized set of 151 genes (Omilian et al., 2020)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Elevated expression of VEGF-activated genes and proliferation-associated gene signature has been associated with AA-TNBC.
source: No significant differences are reported in somatic mutations between AA-TNBC and WA-TNBC in a customized set of 151 genes (Omilian et al., 2020) but elevated expression of VEGF-activated genes and proliferation-associated gene signature, altered TP53, NFB1, and AKT pathways and increased microvessel density has been associated with AA-TNBC (Davis et al., 2020; Lindner et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Altered TP53, NFB1, and AKT pathways have been associated with AA-TNBC.
source: No significant differences are reported in somatic mutations between AA-TNBC and WA-TNBC in a customized set of 151 genes (Omilian et al., 2020) but elevated expression of VEGF-activated genes and proliferation-associated gene signature, altered TP53, NFB1, and AKT pathways and increased microvessel density has been associated with AA-TNBC (Davis et al., 2020; Lindner et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Increased microvessel density has been associated with AA-TNBC.
source: No significant differences are reported in somatic mutations between AA-TNBC and WA-TNBC in a customized set of 151 genes (Omilian et al., 2020) but elevated expression of VEGF-activated genes and proliferation-associated gene signature, altered TP53, NFB1, and AKT pathways and increased microvessel density has been associated with AA-TNBC (Davis et al., 2020; Lindner et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Irrespective of stage at diagnosis, AA-TNBC is more aggressive with higher metastasis and a poorer survival than WA-TNBC.
source: While TNBC biology that drives the aggressive progression of AA-TNBC is still imprecise, it is clear that irrespective of stage at diagnosis, AA-TNBC is more aggressive with higher metastasis and a poorer survival than WA-TNBC.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about AA-TNBC outcomes.

claim: GLI1 is overexpressed in breast cancer stem cells characterized by CD44+/CD24- phenotype compared to other cancer cells.
source: GLI1 is overexpressed in BCSCs characterized by CD44+/CD24- phenotype compared to other cancer cells (Liu et al., 2006)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: GLI1 is important for EMT and metastatic progression.
source: GLI1 is overexpressed in BCSCs characterized by CD44+/CD24- phenotype compared to other cancer cells (Liu et al., 2006) and is important for EMT and metastatic progression (Colavito et al., 2014; Riaz et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Inhibiting sonic hedgehog pathway and GLI1 nuclear localization abrogates CD44+/CD24- positive cell population in TNBC.
source: Inhibiting sonic hedgehog pathway and GLI1 nuclear localization abrogates CD44+/CD24- positive cell population in TNBC (Koike et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: GLI1 associates with increased angiogenesis in TNBC as GLI1 overexpression pairs with VEGFR2 and its inhibition reduces tumor angiogenesis.
source: GLI1 also associates with increased angiogenesis in TNBC as GLI1 overexpression pairs with VEGFR2 and its inhibition reduces tumor angiogenesis (Di Mauro et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: GLI1 preferentially promotes growth of ER-negative breast cancer cells and is associated with poorer survival with TNBC compared to ER-positive disease.
source: Although expressed in many subtypes of breast cancer, GLI1 preferentially promotes growth of ER-negative breast cancer cells and is associated with poorer survival with TNBC compared to ER-positive disease (Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Notch1 plays an important role in maintenance of breast cancer stem cells, EMT, and metastasis.
source: Notch1 can regulate these properties as it plays an important role in maintenance of BCSCs, EMT, as well as metastasis (Kim et al., 2019; Xie et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Overexpression of Notch1 overlaps with ALDH1 expression in breast cancer tissues and significantly correlates with high grade, metastasis, and TNBC.
source: Overexpression of Notch1 overlaps with ALDH1 expression in breast cancer tissues and significantly correlates with high grade, metastasis, and TNBC (Zhong et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A positive correlation exists between EMT-related genes and Notch1 activation in TNBC tumors.
source: A recent study shows a positive correlation between EMT-related genes and Notch1 activation in TNBC tumors (Miao et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Positive association between Notch1 and EMT activator-melanoma cell adhesion molecule denotes its role in EMT progression in TNBC.
source: Positive association between Notch1 and EMT activator-melanoma cell adhesion molecule also denotes its role in EMT progression in TNBC, and accordingly, Notch1 inhibition reverses EMT (Zeng et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Notch1 inhibition reverses EMT in TNBC.
source: Positive association between Notch1 and EMT activator-melanoma cell adhesion molecule also denotes its role in EMT progression in TNBC, and accordingly, Notch1 inhibition reverses EMT (Zeng et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Cancer stem-like cells obtained from AA-TNBC cell line show increased self-renewal.
source: Indeed, cancer stem-like cells obtained from AA-TNBC cell line show increased self-renewal (Yin et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: 48% TNBC in African women exhibit high ALDH+ population compared to non-African women where only 19–30% TNBC show high ALDH + population.
source: Also, 48% TNBC in African women exhibit high ALDH+ population compared to non-African women where only 19–30% TNBC show high ALDH + population (Ginestier et al., 2007; Nalwoga et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: AA- and WA-TNBC tumors have similar mutational profile.
source: A comprehensive analysis of AA- and WA-TNBC tumors report that mutational landscape cannot explain the racial disparity between AA- and WA-TNBC as they have similar mutational profile (Ademuyiwa et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: AA women exhibit higher tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cell density compared to white women.
source: AA women exhibit higher tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cell density compared to white women indicating a potential involvement of immune landscape in racial disparity.
evidence: This statement is based on published literature and involves inference about immune involvement.

claim: Higher CD8+ T cell density in AA-TNBC associates with better overall survival.
source: Although no clear association is observed between CD8+ T cell density and overall survival, higher CD8+ T cell density in AA-TNBC associate with better overall survival which is paradoxical (Abdou et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Exosome analysis shows higher expression of exosomal-Annexin 2 (exo-AnxA2) in the sera of AA women with TNBC indicating its potential role in angiogenesis and tumor promotion.
source: Interestingly, exosome analysis shows higher expression of exosomal-Annexin 2 (exo-AnxA2) in the sera of AA women with TNBC indicating its potential role in angiogenesis and tumor promotion (Chaudhary et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature and involves speculation about biological role.

claim: Proteome profiling of AA- and WA-TNBC exhibit very few alterations in proteins with HSP71 and HNRNP A2/B1 among the most altered proteins.
source: On the other hand, proteome profiling of AA- and WA-TNBC exhibit very few alterations in proteins with HSP71 and HNRNP A2/B1 among the most altered proteins (Torres-Luquis et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: AA- and WA-TNBC tumors show differential expression of Kaiso, which has been linked with increased TNBC aggressiveness.
source: AA- and WA-TNBC tumors show differential expression of Kaiso, which has also been linked with increased TNBC aggressiveness (Bassey-Archibong et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: GLI1 translocates to nucleus upon activation enabling the transcription of GLI1-responsive genes.
source: GLI1, the effector molecule of oncogenic hedgehog-GLI1 pathway, translocates to nucleus upon activation enabling the transcription of GLI1-responsive genes (Bhateja et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature and represents established knowledge about GLI1 function.

claim: Membrane-bound Notch receptor undergoes cleavage upon activation and releases the cytoplasmic domain or Notch intracellular domain (NICD), which translocates to the nucleus and mediates transcriptional activation of Notch-responsive genes.
source: Membrane-bound Notch receptor undergoes cleavage upon activation and releases the cytoplasmic domain or Notch intracellular domain (NICD), which translocates to the nucleus and mediates transcriptional activation of Notch-responsive genes (Brzozowa-Zasada et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature and represents established knowledge about Notch signaling.

claim: Nuclear translocation of NICD is the hallmark of induced Notch signaling cascade.
source: As nuclear translocation of NICD is the hallmark of induced Notch signaling cascade (Brzozowa-Zasada et al., 2017), we analyzed the nuclear localization of Notch1 in multiple AA-TNBC and WA-TNBC cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature and represents established knowledge.
